tldr: Without using any demonstrations or reference trajectories, a humanoid learns to stand up smoothly from deep-seated postures using pure reinforcement learning. Combining biomechanics-inspired staged rewards with a coupled curriculum linking pelvis-assist force and chair height achieves a high success rate of over 97% across eight chair heights.
hero_caption: Learned natural sit-to-stand motion (left) and sampling of diverse initial sitting postures generated using IK (right). The robot achieves motion close to human biomechanics: leaning forward from a deep seat to build momentum, transferring its center of mass to double-foot support, and standing up.
overview:
For humanoid robots, the sit-to-stand (STS) motion involves contact discontinuities as the base of support shifts from the seat to both feet, making it an extremely challenging control problem. Existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have often been limited to rising from shallow seating at the edge of a chair where most body weight is pre-loaded onto the feet, or they produced abrupt, jerky motions when starting from deep-seated postures.

To address this, the authors propose a method that generates smooth sit-to-stand motions from scratch from deep-seated postures using pure reinforcement learning (PPO), without relying on human motion capture data or reference trajectories. There are three key ideas. First, inverse kinematics (IK) is used to generate a large volume of geometrically viable sitting postures, ensuring initial posture diversity. Second, a dimensionless rise-fraction independent of chair height is defined, allowing staged reward functions based on human STS biomechanics for angular momentum generation and center of pressure (COP) attraction. Third, a coupled curriculum is introduced that pairs the decay of vertical pelvis-assisting force with the progressive unlocking of chair heights.

Evaluated on the 29-DoF humanoid "Unitree G1" in simulation (MuJoCo), the policy recorded an outstanding balanced-standing success rate of 97.8% across all eight chair heights in deterministic force-free tests. Ablation studies also revealed that normalization via rise-fraction and progressive chair unlocking play critical roles in generalization and motion smoothness.
contributions: Established a method to synthesize smooth humanoid sit-to-stand motion from deep-seated postures using pure reinforcement learning, without reference motions or imitation learning.

Proposed a dimensionless rise-fraction that normalizes geometric differences across chair heights, enabling unified application of biomechanics-inspired staged rewards (angular momentum control and COP attraction).
Achieved strong generalization while avoiding premature distribution shifts via a coupled curriculum that synchronizes pelvis-assist force decay with progressive chair-height unlocking.
Constructed a large-scale IK-based posture library (29,260 postures) to enable learning from diverse sitting and standing configurations free of physical penetration.

sections.heading: Why is standing up so difficult for a humanoid?
sections.summary: Because humanoid sit-to-stand (STS) motion is contact-rich and highly redundant, conventional optimization and RL methods have often resulted in unnatural motions or remained limited to shallow seating. This paper proposes a new RL-based approach that generates natural rising from deep seating without reference trajectories.
sections.details:
For humanoids operating in human environments, standing up from a chair is an unavoidable task. However, STS involves drastic contact transitions between the seat and foot soles, and there are infinitely many ways to stand up while maintaining balance, making it a formidable control problem.

Prior research broadly falls into four categories:
- Pure trajectory optimization: Because of contact discontinuities, the problem must be divided into multiple phases; methods like MPC often yield jerky, spasmic motions.
- Trajectory optimization with reference motions: These retarget human motion capture data, but bridging dynamic and geometric discrepancies between humans and robots remains difficult.
- Pure reinforcement learning: Policies learn from environmental interaction, but maintaining high success often requires restricting initial states (such as sitting shallowly on the edge of the seat), causing performance to drop significantly under posture variations.
- Reinforcement learning with reference motions (imitation learning): Motions tend to become abrupt, making it difficult to reproduce smooth human-like center-of-mass shifts.

In short, existing methods suffer from two major flaws: relying on shallow sitting where weight is already pre-loaded on the feet, or producing abrupt and violent motions when attempting to rise from deep seating.

To tackle this, the authors combine physics-based reward design inspired by biomechanics, a large contact-consistent posture library using IK, and a coupled curriculum linking assisting force with chair heights, successfully learning smooth and safe rising motions without reference trajectories.

sections.heading: How the biomechanics rewards and coupled curriculum work
sections.summary: Using the 29-DoF Unitree G1, the authors built a PPO reinforcement learning framework. Its core comprises roughly 30,000 IK-generated sitting postures, staged rewards structured by rise-fraction, and a curriculum synchronizing assisting force decay with chair height.
sections.details:
This study uses MuJoCo as the simulator and targets the 29-DoF humanoid robot "Unitree G1". The control policy is trained using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimisation) taking only proprioceptive sensory inputs.

Observation and Action Spaces:
The policy input is a 97-dimensional vector containing the torso gravity projection vector (3D), angular velocity (3D) and linear acceleration (3D) from the IMU, joint positions and velocities for all 29 joints (29D each), previous-step actions (29D), and an action-scaling scalar $\beta_{\max}$ (1D). The policy outputs target joint position increments ($\Delta q$), which are converted into joint torques through PD controllers. The control frequency is 50 Hz.

Large-Scale Posture Generation via IK:
Adding noise directly in joint space causes physical penetration artifacts where the feet or pelvis penetrate the chair, so the authors employed whole-body IK. By randomly varying the seat anterior-posterior position, torso pitch, and foot placements, they pre-generated a library of 29,260 valid sitting postures across eight chair heights. This prevents the policy from merely memorizing a single trajectory.

Rise-Fraction and Staged Rewards:
Phase transitions based on absolute head height fail when chair heights vary. Thus, the authors defined a dimensionless rise-fraction $\rho = (h_{\mathrm{head}} - h_0) / \max(h_{\mathrm{stand}} - h_0, \epsilon) \in [0, 1]$ using the initial seated head height $h_0$ and standing height $h_{\mathrm{stand}}$.
Based on $\rho$, rewards are split into three biomechanics-inspired phases:
- Early rising ($\rho < 0.1$): To promote seat-off, a bonus is given for forward pitch angular velocity $\omega_y |\omega_y|$.
- Mid-rising ($0.1 \leq \rho < 0.8$): A reward attracts the centre of pressure (COP) from the seat toward the foot support region.
- Balanced standing ($\rho \geq 0.8$): The COP is attracted to the geometric center of the double-foot support polygon, and pitch angular velocity is damped.
Additionally, "anti-parking penalties" punish unintended contacts (such as shins or thighs contacting the seat or ground), alongside penalties that preserve actuation smoothness.

Coupled Curriculum:
During early training, an upward vertical assist force $F_{\max}$ (initially 200 N) is applied to the pelvis to aid exploration, while an action-scaling factor $\beta_{\max}$ (initially 1.0) constrains actions. When the standing success rate exceeds a threshold, a gate is passed: $F_{\max}$ decays by 20 N and $\beta_{\max}$ shrinks by 0.02. Rather than expanding from tall chairs (easy conditions) down to short chairs as assistance decays, taller chairs are progressively unlocked as decaying assistance forces policies to master trajectories at each height first. This coupled schedule avoids premature distribution shifts that could collapse the policy.

sections.heading: Achieving a 97.8% success rate and human-like torque and load transfer
sections.summary: In deterministic evaluations without assist forces, the policy achieved a 97.8% sit-to-stand success rate across all eight chair heights. Joint torques remained within safe limits, and the COP shifted naturally from the seat to the foot center.
sections.details:
Trained policies were evaluated in a deterministic simulation environment with all external assisting forces turned off. Performance was assessed across eight chair-height lanes with 50 resets each (400 trials total).

Key Results and Motion Analysis:
- Overall sit-to-stand success reached 97.8%, with an average rising time of 3.54 s and energy consumption of 115.6 J.
- The safety score against torque limits $S_\tau$ was 1.00 (100% within limits), showing that the robot stands up with reasonable actuator torque distributions.
- Sagittal-plane torque profiles show that knees and hips produce appropriate torques around seat-off (~0.5 s) to generate forward angular momentum. Furthermore, an arm-swing synergy emerged naturally to build momentum, despite no explicit arm-driving rewards.
- COP trajectories confirmed that ground reaction forces initially located near the pelvis-seat contact point swiftly transferred into the double-foot support base during rising, ultimately settling at the center of the feet.

Ablation Findings:
- Replacing the rise-fraction with absolute head height eliminated chair-height normalization, causing a major drop in performance.
- Training on all chair heights mixed together from the start (schedule-off) failed to cope with rapid distribution shifts during assistance decay, lowering success rates.
- Removing the pitch angular momentum reward reduced seat-off momentum and lowered success, while removing the COP attraction reward caused more than a 2x increase in action jitter despite successful rising. This proves COP guidance is essential for smooth load transfer.

Limitations and Challenges:
When initial foot positions were extremely close to the chair edge (around 2–3 cm), the robot occasionally exhibited unnatural behavior, pressing its legs against the chair for leverage. Moreover, while 90% of the motion completes within 3–4 seconds, fully settling into quiet standing takes up to 5 seconds, leaving room to improve terminal convergence speed.

sections.heading: Conclusions and prospects for real-robot deployment
sections.summary: Biomechanics-inspired rewards and a coupled curriculum enabled natural and robust humanoid sit-to-stand motions via reinforcement learning without reference trajectories. Future work looks toward sim-to-real transfer.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated that the challenging contact-transition problem of a humanoid robot autonomously rising from deep-seated postures can be solved through pure reinforcement learning.

The keys to success were integrating a large-scale IK posture library free of penetration artifacts, a dimensionless rise-fraction absorbing chair-height discrepancies, biomechanics-inspired rewards regulating COP and angular momentum, and a coupled curriculum unlocking chair heights alongside assist decay. Together, these allowed a single PPO policy to achieve over 97% success and smooth torque profiles across eight chair heights.

For future work, the authors plan to build on these simulation results by applying domain randomization and testing sit-to-stand motions on real humanoid hardware (Sim-to-Real).

takeaways: In reinforcement learning with discontinuous contact transitions, sampling initial states via whole-body IK rather than joint-space noise is crucial to prevent geometric penetration artifacts.
When task geometry changes (such as chair height), staging reward phases using a dimensionless progress metric (rise-fraction) instead of absolute coordinates is key to generalization.
COP attraction rewards act as powerful regularizers that suppress joint action jitter and promote smooth weight transfer, beyond just improving success rates.

When increasing task difficulty, coupling assist force decay with gated progressive unlocking of environmental difficulty (chair height) prevents catastrophic policy collapse and premature distribution shifts.
limitations: Validation is currently confined to MuJoCo simulations, without physical Sim-to-Real demonstration on real humanoid hardware.
When initial foot placement is too close to the chair edge (a 2–3 cm gap), the robot rarely exhibits unnatural behavior by bracing its legs against the chair.
Although 90% of the movement completes in 3–4 seconds, coming to a complete, stable stop takes up to 5 seconds, making terminal settling relatively slow.
